newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Snake charmers, fire eaters still a Coney Island draw.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Snake charmers, fire eaters still a Coney Island draw.

text.p: Sometimes the python is too cranky to be charmed and a few months back the fire-swallowing "Queen of Kerosone" went on maternity leave.

Running a sideshow has never been easy, not for P.T. Barnum more than 100 years ago, and certainly not today in the age of television and the Internet. But no one in the rare troupe that performs in this legendary amusement park expects diamond days when they are trying to keep alive the old-time theatrical hustle of the sideshow.

"It's a struggle, but it's worth it," Dick Zigun, the 43-year old founder of Sideshows by the Seashore said. The sideshow, made popular by Barnum in 1842, traditionally has been the stage for freaks and a cast a nimble characters who contort, swallow swords or nap on a bed of nails.

At his American Museum in New York, Barnum gained fame when he showed the gawkers such proteges as "General Tom Thumb," "JoJo the Dog-Faced Boy" and the original "Siamese Twins." Today, Zigun shies away from hiring the disabled, relying instead on New York's seemingly endless gallery of eccentrics and artists to keep alive what remains a peculiar sort of popular theatre.

"I wanted to take a serious, curious look at this really off-beat form of entertainment that reflects the wacky forms of American culture," the Yale Drama School graduate said. And for Zigun there is no better place to perform than Coney Island, once America's best known amusement park where Thomas Edison electrocuted an elephant in 1903 to prove the efficacy of direct current.

"Coney Island has this incredible history. First time I visited, the sand just stayed in my shoes," said Zigun, who hails from Barnum's hometown, Bridgeport, Connecticut. On a pedestal outside the theatre on a recent evening, a barker in a bowler hat shouted out the age-old sideshow ballyhoo: "Step right up folks and see all that will astonish and amaze you."

And step up they do. Since Zigun opened his show on the boardwalk along the Atlantic Ocean 12 years ago, 30,000 to 70,000 people a year have seen the one-hour presentations, which run yearly from mid-May to mid-September.
"This place still has that magic of the past," said Enchantra, the snake charmer who sometimes doubles as the Elastic Lady.

Inside, seated on a rough wooden grandstand, Zigun's paying customers watch as Enchantra becomes a human pretzel and avoids being mangled by steel blades inserted through a coffin-like box into which she has been strapped. Then comes the King of Kerosene swallowing flames and a lady with a beard who juggles very sharp knives.
It feels like a day at the circus, but the show does not always run smoothly.

The pay is low and Zigun has been so strapped for cash he lost what had been a prime boardwalk location for one of lesser prestige. There is a also high rate of attrition -- Manhattan remains a beacon for eccentrics and Zigun's "freaks" tend to come and go.
"Our longest-running performer has stayed about six years," Zigun said. "It's sometimes hard to find performers, it's not like we advertise in the New York Times."

Recently the former Queen of Kerosene, Kiva Szczepanski, left to have a child -- her second by her husband, the Human Blockhead, among whose talents are hammering five-inch nails up into his nose. Then, this last summer, Zigun's principal attraction, The World's Most Illustrated Man (boasting 25,000 tattoos), died after a long struggle with diabetes.
But just like "The Fantasticks," "Cats" or any other long-running on or off-Broadway performance, Zigun says, the show must go on. If only that 15-foot Albino python behaves.
